title: Forecasting horizontal gene transfer and resistance spread in microbial communities

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to forecast which genes will move between microbes, which recipients will acquire them, and whether those genes will persist and spread as community conditions change. Horizontal gene transfer allows microbes to acquire genetic material outside parent-to-offspring inheritance. A useful forecast would distinguish an initial transfer event from successful establishment: receiving a resistance gene does not guarantee that the recipient will retain it or that resistance will become widespread.

The capability would connect transfer machinery, compatibility between a mobile element and its host, opportunities for donor–recipient contact, environmental selection, and the mechanisms that maintain or remove acquired DNA. Genome inventories provide part of this information, but do not fully describe those changing processes. The supplied evidence grounds this formulation in plasmid biology; extending forecasts to other mobile genetic elements and transfer systems remains part of the proposed scope.

As a proposed modeling goal, forecasts should express probabilities and uncertainty over specified time horizons and environmental conditions. They could estimate how a defined intervention changes transfer and persistence risk without claiming an exact deterministic time for every event.

significance.text: Reliable forecasts would make antimicrobial-resistance surveillance more prospective: alongside identifying resistance genes and mobile elements already present, researchers could estimate which are likely to move and become established. Resistance genes are biologically relevant cargo for this goal. The supplied study reports antibiotic resistance as the most frequent functional category among its annotated plasmid cargo genes and experimentally demonstrates resistance delivery in a selected transfer experiment.

The direct benefit, if the capability were validated, would be better estimates of transfer and establishment risk under specified conditions. As a conditional downstream possibility, those estimates could help prioritize surveillance and compare interventions before resistance becomes widespread. Preventing clinical resistance would additionally require effective surveillance, stewardship, feasible interventions, and successful implementation; predictive accuracy alone would not establish a clinical benefit. The supplied evidence neither tests these benefits nor quantifies their eventual magnitude.

The potentially transformative advance is a connection between microbial genetics, ecology, evolution, and resistance epidemiology that generalizes beyond the examples used to construct a model. Its reach would depend on the environments, organisms, elements, and interventions for which it remains reliable. A successful forecast in one gut-associated plasmid system would provide a bounded achievement, not evidence of universal prediction across microbial communities.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an experimentally validated connection from biological mechanisms and ecological conditions to future transfer and subsequent persistence. Plasmid backbones can encode replication and transfer machinery, and compatibility and maintenance affect whether an element can remain in a host. Environmental pressures can also favor plasmid gain or loss. Combining these mechanisms into a forecast requires explaining how they interact as community composition and conditions change.

A concrete measurement barrier is establishing which mobile elements are present and associating them with the biological entities whose behavior must be predicted. The supplied study acknowledges false positives, false negatives, and fragmented sequences in plasmid identification. Those uncertainties matter because an incomplete or incorrect starting inventory can distort estimates of both transfer opportunities and persistence. Better sequence classification is therefore an enabling component, while forecasting also requires observations of contact, acquisition, retention, and loss over time.

As an engineering synthesis, the challenge is to build models that separate the probability of transfer from the probability of establishment, propagate uncertainty in their inputs, and remain calibrated on previously untested elements and communities. Intervention forecasts must also distinguish a change caused by the intervention from a correlation in existing sequence distributions. The supplied record does not establish that these capabilities have been achieved generally, and it does not provide a sufficiently current field survey to determine their full status in November 2026.

current_state.text: In the study published on 4 March 2024, Michael K. Yu, Emily C. Fogarty, and A. Murat Eren used PlasX and MobMess to identify and organize candidate plasmids from human gut metagenomes. Applying MobMess to sequences predicted by PlasX yielded 1,169 plasmid systems. This demonstrates large-scale identification and organization within that dataset and biological setting; the count is not a count of experimentally confirmed transfers or successful forecasts.

The researchers also experimentally confirmed transfer of a selected predicted plasmid from Bacteroides fragilis p-214 to B. fragilis 638R, with delivery of erythromycin resistance. The supplied review reports that the methods describe dual-antibiotic selection, donor-only and recipient-only controls, and sequencing of transconjugants. These observations support a specific laboratory transfer and resistance-delivery result. They do not establish persistence in a complex community or predict future spread across communities.

The methods and initial validation account identify the transferred plasmid as pFIJ0137_1, while other article sections use pFIJ1037_1. The supplied review leaves that identifier discrepancy unresolved. It does not undermine the supported description of a selected transfer experiment, but it matters for precise cross-referencing or replication of the named construct. More broadly, predicted plasmids remain candidates because classification errors and fragmented assemblies can affect the inventory.

The evidence assessment supplied with this record used a verified, untruncated alternative full-text XML of the article, including methods and references. Linked supplementary materials and figure images were not supplied for inspection. The assessment of the selected transfer rests on the described methods rather than on independently inspected supplementary figures. These access boundaries should be retained when interpreting the level of experimental detail available here.

The supplied record contains no freshness-search entries establishing the field's latest capabilities as of 1 November 2026. It therefore supports a dated 2024 achievement in gut-plasmid identification and selected experimental validation, while leaving the present breadth of forecasting capabilities unresolved. That evidence limitation does not show that later forecasting results are absent or that the reported 2024 findings are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: make blinded predictions across independently selected communities and environments, including mobile elements and resistance genes not used to develop the model. Specify recipients or recipient groups, environmental conditions, interventions, and prediction horizons in advance. Evaluate transfer and subsequent persistence as separate outcomes, so that observing acquisition alone cannot count as successful prediction of lasting spread.
completion_criteria.label: Blinded predictions distinguish transfer from persistence across independent communities

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: use longitudinal sampling and experimental tracing to establish whether predicted acquisitions, retention, and losses occur. Compare results with simple baselines, such as forecasts based on starting prevalence or observed host associations, and report both predictive accuracy and probability calibration. A convincing protocol should define calibration metrics, baseline choices, acceptable performance, and handling of uncertain or undetected events before outcomes are known. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Longitudinal tracing validates forecast accuracy and calibration against predefined baselines

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat evaluations with independent datasets, experiments, and investigators, and disclose the measurements required to make each forecast. Report performance separately across biological settings and identify conditions where the model fails or becomes poorly calibrated. Successful finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries; they would not establish literal universality. Exact deterministic timing is unnecessary if probabilistic forecasts reliably support the decisions they are intended to inform.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reports required measurements and setting-specific performance limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed impact validation should remain separate from scientific forecasting validation. Demonstrating that predictions improve surveillance priorities or intervention choices would strengthen practical value. Demonstrating prevention of clinical resistance would require additional outcome evidence linking those choices to reduced resistance or disease burden.
completion_criteria.label: Separate impact validation demonstrates improved surveillance priorities or intervention choices

related_concepts.text: MIC-02, A predictive theory of microbial communities, has the closest overlap: community composition and ecological interactions shape opportunities for gene movement. MIC-09 focuses specifically on the acquisition, maintenance, and spread of mobile genetic material and resistance traits. A community model might supply ecological inputs without accurately predicting transfer, while a transfer model could succeed within a bounded community setting without explaining community dynamics generally.

MIC-06, A predictive whole-cell model for microbial design, overlaps through the intracellular consequences of acquiring and maintaining new genetic material. Its primary target is cellular behavior and design, whereas MIC-09 connects gene movement to outcomes across populations and communities. MIC-03, Routine experimental access to microbial dark matter, could broaden the organisms available for testing transfer predictions, but experimental access alone does not supply a forecasting capability.

MIC-07, Programmable, reversible living therapies in the human microbiome, and MIC-10, Programmable microbial consortia for durable ecosystem functions, could benefit from understanding whether introduced genetic traits remain in intended hosts or spread elsewhere. MIC-04, Reliable nitrogen-fixing microbial partnerships for major cereal crops, offers a distinct potential application setting for questions about trait maintenance and movement. These concepts concern designed therapies or sustained functions; MIC-09 concerns forecasting genetic movement and persistence, whether beneficial, harmful, or neutral.

MIC-08, Broadly effective control of bacterial antibiotic persistence, addresses a different resistance-related problem. Persistence concerns survival during antibiotic exposure and should not be equated with horizontal acquisition of resistance genes. MIC-05, A general platform for targeted, adaptable phage treatment, overlaps with microbial host compatibility and evolutionary response, but treatment performance remains a separate goal from forecasting mobile-element spread.

MIC-11, Quantifying how environmental viruses control biogeochemical fluxes, shares an interest in ecological consequences involving viruses, while targeting ecosystem fluxes rather than gene-transfer forecasts. MIC-12, A causal map from microbial metabolites to host phenotypes, targets effects mediated by metabolites. MIC-01, An autonomously reproducing cell built from defined components, targets cell construction. These roster distinctions are conceptual comparisons based on the supplied titles; the supplied plasmid study does not establish achievements for those other innovations.

unresolved_issues: No supplied freshness-search record establishes the field's latest capabilities as of 1 November 2026; the current openness and breadth of the forecasting problem remain unresolved.
The pFIJ0137_1 versus pFIJ1037_1 identifier discrepancy remains unresolved.
Linked supplementary materials and figure images were not supplied for inspection in the review.
Generalization beyond the documented human-gut plasmid setting, including other mobile elements, communities, and environments, remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
An operational forecasting benchmark still needs prediction horizons, calibration metrics, baseline definitions, acceptable performance, and procedures for uncertain observations.
The feasibility and eventual clinical impact of broadly generalizable forecasts are not established or quantified by the supplied study.

brief.title: Forecasts of how antibiotic resistance spreads
possible: Researchers could forecast which genes microbes will pass to their neighbours, which microbes will receive them, and whether the genes will stay and spread. Forecasts would give probabilities for specified conditions and time periods.
They could also estimate how an intervention changes those risks. A forecast would distinguish a resistance gene arriving in a microbe from that gene becoming established in the community.
why: Resistance surveillance could look ahead. Researchers could identify genes likely to spread and establish themselves, helping them prioritise monitoring and compare interventions before resistance becomes widespread.

sources.who: Michael K. Yu, Emily C. Fogarty and A. Murat Eren
sources.showed: They grouped predicted plasmids, pieces of DNA that can move between cells, into 1,169 related systems in human gut samples. They also confirmed a selected plasmid's transfer and delivery of antibiotic resistance in the laboratory.
sources.quote: Individual plasmids were often country specific, yet most plasmid systems spanned across geographically distinct human populations.
sources.cited_for: Identifying plasmids and confirming a selected transfer provide starting points for forecasting.
sources.not_established: The study does not demonstrate forecasts of future transfer or lasting spread across communities.

sources.showed: They showed that plasmids can persist without antibiotics because transfer between cells offsets their costs and loss. A model predicted persistence in laboratory communities.
sources.quote: Here, we show that common conjugal plasmids covering major incompatibility groups and a range of fitness burdens can be maintained via conjugation
sources.cited_for: Measured transfer, growth costs and DNA loss can support predictions of plasmid persistence.
sources.not_established: Laboratory persistence predictions leave reliability across unfamiliar natural communities unresolved.

sources.showed: They tracked shared DNA in gut samples collected years apart. They found that gene exchange and replacement of bacterial strains both contribute to the spread of mobile genes.
sources.quote: Notably, HGT and strain replacement act together to disseminate mobile genes in the population.
sources.cited_for: Tracking communities over time reveals how mobile genes persist and spread.
sources.not_established: Observing changes over time does not establish accurate advance predictions of future transfers.

sources.showed: Experiments and simulations showed that growth after plasmid acquisition helps determine which microbes carry it. Faster growth produced more recipient cells but less recipient diversity.
sources.quote: Fast-growth conditions increased transconjugant abundance but reduced diversity, whereas slow-growth conditions supported fewer but more diverse transconjugants.
sources.cited_for: Forecasting spread requires accounting for both DNA transfer and the subsequent growth of recipient cells.
sources.not_established: These results do not establish reliable forecasts across different communities and changing environments.

shown: Lopatkin and colleagues predicted plasmid persistence in laboratory communities and showed how targeting transfer and DNA loss could reverse resistance. Yu and colleagues mapped candidate gut plasmids and confirmed a selected resistance-delivering transfer.
Peng and colleagues tracked mobile genes in human gut communities over time. Takahashi and colleagues showed that growth conditions change the abundance and diversity of plasmid recipients.
missing: Blind tests must predict both acquisition and lasting retention in unfamiliar communities under changing conditions.
Forecasts need reliable starting inventories that link mobile DNA to its microbial hosts.
Predicted intervention effects need experiments that establish cause and effect.
Independent tests must establish where forecasts remain reliable and whether they improve decisions.

milestones.label: Blind predictions distinguish transfer from lasting retention
milestones.explanation: Blind tests would have to predict acquisition and persistence separately across independent communities, including unfamiliar genes and specified conditions. This would test whether forecasts generalise.

milestones.label: Tracking confirms accuracy and reliable probabilities
milestones.explanation: Repeated sampling and experimental tracing would have to beat simple forecasts and show that predicted odds match observed frequencies under predefined criteria. This would establish measurable forecasting skill.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and identify limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat evaluations, report required measurements and identify settings where predictions fail. This would establish the capability's demonstrated reach.

milestones.label: Forecasts improve surveillance or intervention choices
milestones.explanation: Separate impact studies would have to show that forecasts improve monitoring priorities or intervention choices. This would establish practical value, with reduced clinical resistance requiring further outcome evidence.

uncertain: How far can forecasts generalise beyond tested plasmids, organisms and environments?
Which prediction periods, simple comparisons and accuracy thresholds would make forecasts useful?
Would forecast-guided choices ultimately reduce resistance or disease?

page.title: Forecasting plasmid-mediated resistance in gut bacterial networks
page.definition: A model predicts whether antibiotic-resistance plasmids, transferable DNA molecules, sustain transmission within and between human gut bacterial communities during and after antibiotic use.

goal.need: Bacterial antimicrobial resistance accounted for an estimated 1.14 million deaths worldwide in 2021 (95% uncertainty interval, 1.00–1.28 million). This estimate covers bacterial resistance overall, rather than deaths attributed specifically to plasmid transmission.

statements.quote: predict whether a plasmid carrying antibiotic resistance genes (pARG) has epidemic-like potential
strengthen surveillance systems and laboratory networks to inform effective, evidence-driven antimicrobial resistance policies and actions;
statements.context: An objective of the updated Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, described in WHO’s fact sheet dated 16 July 2026.

completion.title: A model classifies epidemic plasmid spread with ≥80% balanced predictive accuracy at each of five sites.
completion.criterion: A coupled model of within-gut and between-person transmission classifies whether resistance-carrying plasmids exceed R₀ = 1, the threshold for sustained transmission, with ≥80% balanced predictive accuracy at each of five sites during and after antibiotic use.
completion.set_by: Wellcome Leap, Resistance Networks programme announcement, Thrust 1A; a funder-defined research test.
completion.basis: The programme sets a numerical prediction target for gut Enterobacterales across bacterial cells and people.

milestones.title: A model correctly predicts persistence of nine plasmids in E. coli for 14–20 days.
milestones.criterion: Measured conjugation, plasmid loss and fitness effects predict persistence of nine plasmids from six incompatibility groups. Each persists in mixed plasmid-bearing and plasmid-free E. coli populations without antibiotic selection, with 10,000-fold daily dilution for 14–20 days. Lopatkin et al. reported this result on 22 November 2017; experiments were repeated at least twice, with four to six plating measurements per determination.
milestones.set_by: Lopatkin et al., published laboratory validation protocol, Figure 2d; a study-specific test.
milestones.threshold_quote: Daily dilutions were performed for 14–20 days.

milestones.title: Single-cell sequencing links resistance genes, plasmids and hosts with ≥95% concordance.
milestones.criterion: Assignments achieve ≥95% agreement with complete long-read sequencing on the programme’s Enterobacterales reference panel, resolving mobile elements, all plasmids and host chromosomes. An enabling inventory was published by Yu et al. on 4 March 2024: 68,350 candidate plasmids grouped into 1,169 systems from 1,782 human gut metagenomes. That inventory does not establish the linkage-concordance result.
milestones.set_by: Wellcome Leap, Resistance Networks programme announcement, Thrust 2 linkage-accuracy requirement.

milestones.title: Human plasmid transmission estimates have 95% confidence intervals within ±50% of their point estimates.
milestones.criterion: R₀-within and R₀-between estimates under antibiotic pressure each have 95% confidence intervals of ±50% of their point estimates. Peng et al., published on 22 November 2025, analysed 676 fecal samples from 338 people approximately four years apart. They tracked mobile-sequence prevalence and distinguished examples of transfer from strain replacement; they did not report these plasmid-specific R₀ estimates.
milestones.set_by: Wellcome Leap, Resistance Networks programme announcement, Thrusts 1B–1C.

not_found: No common forecasting acceptance test spanning conjugation, transformation and transduction across microbial environments was found.
No published result meeting Resistance Networks’ five-site prediction target was found.
No fixed forecast horizon, probability-calibration threshold or held-out validation split was located in the programme announcement.

results.finding: Across 1,782 human gut metagenomes, PlasX identified 68,350 non-redundant candidate plasmids.
results.detail: MobMess grouped the predicted plasmids into 1,169 systems. The inventory does not establish single-cell linkage of resistance genes, plasmids and hosts or the required concordance with long-read sequencing.
results.quote: Here we developed a machine-learning model, PlasX, which identified 68,350 non-redundant plasmids across human gut metagenomes and organized them into 1,169 evolutionarily cohesive ‘plasmid systems’ using our sequence containment-aware network-partitioning algorithm, MobMess.

results.finding: Predicted persistence was observed for all nine plasmids in E. coli over 14–20 days.
results.detail: The plasmids covered six incompatibility groups. Experiments were repeated at least twice, with four to six plating measurements per determination. The model used the measured loss rate of plasmid K as an assumption for the other plasmids.
results.quote: Daily dilutions were performed for 14–20 days. Indeed, each plasmid persisted throughout the duration of the experiment

results.finding: Among 338 people, prevalence of a β-lactamase-encoding HGT segment rose to 52.1%.
results.detail: Prevalence was 40.5% at baseline. The study tracked mobile-sequence prevalence but did not report plasmid-specific within-person or between-person R₀ estimates and confidence intervals under antibiotic pressure.
results.quote:
Another notable increase in
Anaerobutyricum hallii
was linked to a 5.2-kb segment encoding β-lactamase, with its prevalence rising from 40.5% to 52.1%.

results.finding: Scellmate achieved 100% species-consistent host–mobile element linkages in a four-strain mock dataset of 3,035 single-cell genomes.
results.detail: The benchmark used isolate genome assemblies as ground truth, not complete long-read sequencing of the programme’s Enterobacterales reference panel. It does not establish concordance for resistance genes, all plasmids and host chromosomes.

results.finding: CAP-seq distinguished plasmid-encoded resistance marker patterns across 2,427 E. coli single-cell genomes.
results.detail: The mock-community result links strain-specific plasmid markers to E. coli cells, but does not report assignment concordance against complete long-read sequencing on the programme’s reference panel or resolve all plasmids and mobile elements.
results.quote:
These distinct marker patterns enabled unambiguous strain-level separation, 
assigning 10 SAGs to MACH1 and the remainder to BL21.

results.finding: 16 rectal swabs: all 11 plasmid-encoded carbapenemases were assigned to correct bacterial hosts (11/11, 100%).
results.detail: Partial: not single-cell sequencing; only carbapenemase-carrying plasmids were assessed, not all plasmids/mobile elements; comparison was to isolate WGS/culture, not the programme's Enterobacterales reference panel. Mock contig-level accuracy was 93.8% (15/16).
results.quote: The remaining 11 carbapenemases were predicted to be encoded by plasmid contigs; all of them could be associated with their correct microbial host according to isolate-based established diagnostics and WGS using our css
